props.t: "Just the root and the 5th, with no 3rd, so it is neither major nor minor. With distortion it sounds huge but stays clear: the engine of rock, punk, grunge and metal riffs."
"The bright, settled triad that most music calls home. Root, major 3rd and perfect 5th: the 3rd decides its open, sunny colour."
"The major triad with its 3rd lowered a semitone. That one note moves the colour from open to inward: reflective, serious, sometimes tender."

"A major triad with a minor 7th on top. The 3rd and 7th form a tritone that wants to resolve, so this chord pulls strongly to the chord a 5th below: the engine of the perfect cadence, and the home chord of the blues."
"No 3rd at all: the 2nd stands in its place, so the chord is neither major nor minor. Open, airy and unresolved; loved in pop, rock and film."
"The 4th replaces the 3rd and leans on it, wanting to fall back down a step. Historically a suspension held over from the chord before; now also a colour of its own."
"Two stacked minor 3rds. Tense and unstable, it rarely stays long; it usually acts as a dominant, leading up by step into the chord that follows."

"Two stacked major 3rds. On a piano (equal temperament) it is symmetrical: from the top note up to the root again is a diminished 4th, which sounds the same as a major 3rd, so its three notes split the octave into three equal parts and every inversion sounds like another augmented triad in root position. Dreamlike, it hangs in the air; often a passing chord that pushes a 5th upward by a semitone."
"A major triad with a major 7th a semitone below the octave. That clash makes it lush and bittersweet rather than plain: the sound of bossa nova, neo-soul and late-night ballads."
"A minor triad with a minor 7th: soft, mellow and smooth. A staple of jazz, soul, funk and modal harmony. Its function depends entirely on the key and the chords around it."
"A major triad with an added 6th: sweet, vintage and stable. Swing endings, early rock and roll and film-musical finales."
"A major triad with a 9th added but no 7th. Shimmering and open; a favourite of guitar-based pop and worship music."
"A minor triad with an added 9th and no 7th. Wistful and open: a favourite of singer-songwriters and film scores."
"A minor triad with a major 6th: dark but with a glint of light. Tango, film noir and gypsy jazz; often the home chord of a minor key in jazz."
"A diminished triad with a minor 7th. The ii chord of a minor key: it prepares the dominant in a minor ii–V–i, and its uneasy colour suits suspense."

"Three stacked minor 3rds. Respelled, the same four sounds are the leading-note 7th (vii°7) of four different minor keys a minor 3rd apart, so it can pivot to many keys. Highly unstable and dramatic; a favourite of Romantic opera and silent-film villains."
"A dominant 7th with a 9th on top: fuller and funkier. It still pulls to the chord a 5th below. Funk, soul and blues bands live on it."

"A minor 7th with a 9th: warm, smoky, modal. The opening chord of countless jazz and R&B grooves."

"le, do, re and fi: the Italian sixth plus re."

props.feel: "A full stop. Finished, settled, home."
props.why: "The dominant (V) holds the leading note (ti), which rises a semitone to do, and the bass leaps from so down to do. Tension, then release."
props.where: "The final chords of most hymns, anthems and classical movements, and the end of any chorus that lands firmly on home."

props.feel: "A soft full stop: the \"Amen\" at the end of a hymn."
props.why: "No leading note, so there is no pull, just a gentle settling. fa falls to mi (or le to so in minor) and the bass moves fa → do."
props.where: "Sung \"Amen\"s, gospel endings and rock codas that lean back onto home."

props.feel: "A comma, or a question mark. We have stopped, but we are not home."
props.why: "The phrase pauses on the dominant, so the leading note hangs in the air waiting to resolve. The ear expects an answer."
props.where: "The end of the first phrase in countless songs, folk tunes and classical themes: the question before the answer."

props.feel: "A swerve. We expected home and got somewhere close by but surprising."
props.why: "V sets up I, the leading note still rises to do, but the bass steps up to la instead of falling to do. vi shares two notes with I, so it sounds like home with the lights off."
props.where: "Just before a final chorus or a big ending, to delay the arrival and make the real ending land harder."

props.where: "Baroque slow movements and the end of a slow movement before a fast finale."

props.where: "Classical concertos (just before the cadenza) and the end of many hymns and anthems."

"A major chord a tone below home. No leading note, so the return to I feels open and strong, not polite."

props.d: "One semibreve against each note of the cantus. Every pair must be a consonance, so the whole art is in how the two lines move."
"Two minims against each cantus note. Downbeats are consonant; the weak beat may be a dissonance only as a passing note, moving by step between two consonances."
"Four crotchets against each cantus note. Every downbeat is consonant; a dissonant crotchet must be a passing note, a neighbour note, or part of the cambiata figure."

"The counterpoint is tied across every barline (a ligature), so it always moves half a bar after the cantus. The tied note may clash with the new cantus note (a suspension) and must then fall by step to a consonance."

"Florid counterpoint mixes everything: minims, crotchets, tied notes and pairs of quavers, chosen bar by bar. Each note value keeps the rules of its own species, and suspensions may be decorated before they resolve."
"Two counterpoints against the cantus, note against note."

Understand · AABA, and a wheel of turnarounds

32-bar song form (AABA). Four 8-bar sections: a tune (A), the tune again (A), a contrasting bridge (B, also called the middle eight or release), and the tune once more (A). It is the most common form of the American popular song from about 1925 to 1960, and so of most jazz standards.

Rhythm changes are the chords of George Gershwin's "I Got Rhythm" (1930). Jazz musicians, especially the bebop players of the 1940s, wrote dozens of new melodies over them. Gershwin's own song adds a two-bar tag to the last A (34 bars); jazz players dropped it and play an even 32.

The A section is a wheel of turnarounds: I–vi–ii–V (or I–VI7–ii–V), two bars each, then a trip to IV in bars 5–6 and back. The bridge is a chain of secondary dominants around the cycle of 5ths: III7 → VI7 → II7 → V7, each lasting two bars, each the V7 of the next (see climbs 6 and 7). The last one, V7, leads home into the final A.

Jazz practice. Players treat these chords as a framework, not a fixed list. They substitute freely: a ii7 before each bridge dominant, tritone substitutes (climb 10), passing diminished chords. The checker holds you to the landmarks that make it rhythm changes and calls the rest style.

Understand · strains, repeats and the trio

Ragtime was the popular piano music of the USA from about 1895 to 1920, created mainly by African American composers such as Scott Joplin, James Scott and Eubie Blake. Its right hand is syncopated (accents fall between the beats) against a steady left hand that marches: bass, chord, bass, chord.

The form comes from the march. A rag is built from strains: complete 16-bar tunes, each usually repeated. The common plan is Intro, AA BB A, then the trio CC DD. The trio moves to the subdominant key (IV), as in Sousa's marches. Many rags end in the trio key; some, including "Maple Leaf Rag", return home for the last strain (see its score in the Analysis room). Each strain is itself a small double period: 8 bars ending on V, then 8 bars ending with a perfect cadence (see Phrase, period and sentence).

The harmony is common-practice with a popular accent: chains of secondary dominants (VI7–II7–V7–I), passing diminished chords and borrowed iv. Unlike the blues, the dominant 7ths here do resolve. That is the ragtime sound, and it leads straight into stride piano and early jazz.

Understand · the refrain and the journeys between

A rondo alternates one recurring section, the refrain (A), with contrasting episodes (B, C, D). The refrain always returns in the home key; the episodes travel to other keys. The smallest rondo is five-part, ABACA; a seven-part rondo is ABACABA.

It was the favourite form for the last movement of Classical sonatas, symphonies and concertos (Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven): the refrain is usually a cheerful, catchy tune, and every return is a small homecoming. The refrain itself is often a period or a small binary form (see Phrase, period and sentence). A retransition, often a passage sitting on V7, prepares each return.

Compared with verse and chorus. A pop song's chorus also keeps coming back, so the idea is the same, but the Classical rondo makes the key the point: away in the episodes, home for every refrain.

"No 3rd at all: the 2nd stands in its place, so the chord is neither major nor minor. Open, airy and unresolved; loved in pop, rock and film."
"The 4th replaces the 3rd and leans on it, wanting to fall back down a step. Historically a suspension held over from the chord before; now also a colour of its own."
"Two stacked minor 3rds. Tense and unstable, it rarely stays long; it usually acts as a dominant, leading up by step into the chord that follows."

"Two stacked major 3rds. On a piano (equal temperament) it is symmetrical: from the top note up to the root again is a diminished 4th, which sounds the same as a major 3rd, so its three notes split the octave into three equal parts and every inversion sounds like another augmented triad in root position. Dreamlike, it hangs in the air; often a passing chord that pushes a 5th upward by a semitone."
"A major triad with a major 7th a semitone below the octave. That clash makes it lush and bittersweet rather than plain: the sound of bossa nova, neo-soul and late-night ballads."
"A minor triad with a minor 7th: soft, mellow and smooth. A staple of jazz, soul, funk and modal harmony. Its function depends entirely on the key and the chords around it."

"The most common of all: the dominant gets its own dominant, so the half-way point feels like an arrival."
"A sudden turn towards the relative key: in major it darkens, in minor it brightens."
"Home itself becomes a dominant 7th and tips over into IV. Blues and gospel players do this all the time."
"A brief visit to a chord a step away, then straight back on course."
"The rarest of the five in major: a quick shadow before the music turns back."
"A secondary dominant can interrupt too: V7/vi promises vi and lands on IV instead."
"The other way to point at a chord: a diminished 7th built on its leading note."
"IV turns minor for one chord: la sinks to le. The most bittersweet semitone in pop."
"A major chord a tone below home. No leading note, so the return to I feels open and strong, not polite."
"Two borrowed chords climb by step to home: a heroic, victorious ending."

"The engine of jazz. Two falling 5ths into home, with a 7th on every chord."
"The dark twin: a half-diminished ii, and a V with a flattened 9th borrowed from the minor scale (a flattened 13th joins it at Level 7)."

props.d: "One semibreve against each note of the cantus. Every pair must be a consonance, so the whole art is in how the two lines move."
"Two minims against each cantus note. Downbeats are consonant; the weak beat may be a dissonance only as a passing note, moving by step between two consonances."
"Four crotchets against each cantus note. Every downbeat is consonant; a dissonant crotchet must be a passing note, a neighbour note, or part of the cambiata figure."

"The counterpoint is tied across every barline (a ligature), so it always moves half a bar after the cantus. The tied note may clash with the new cantus note (a suspension) and must then fall by step to a consonance."

"Florid counterpoint mixes everything: minims, crotchets, tied notes and pairs of quavers, chosen bar by bar. Each note value keeps the rules of its own species, and suspensions may be decorated before they resolve."
"Two counterpoints against the cantus, note against note."

Understand · AABA, and a wheel of turnarounds

32-bar song form (AABA). Four 8-bar sections: a tune (A), the tune again (A), a contrasting bridge (B, also called the middle eight or release), and the tune once more (A). It is the most common form of the American popular song from about 1925 to 1960, and so of most jazz standards.

Rhythm changes are the chords of George Gershwin's "I Got Rhythm" (1930). Jazz musicians, especially the bebop players of the 1940s, wrote dozens of new melodies over them. Gershwin's own song adds a two-bar tag to the last A (34 bars); jazz players dropped it and play an even 32.

The A section is a wheel of turnarounds: I–vi–ii–V (or I–VI7–ii–V), two bars each, then a trip to IV in bars 5–6 and back. The bridge is a chain of secondary dominants around the cycle of 5ths: III7 → VI7 → II7 → V7, each lasting two bars, each the V7 of the next (see climbs 6 and 7). The last one, V7, leads home into the final A.

Jazz practice. Players treat these chords as a framework, not a fixed list. They substitute freely: a ii7 before each bridge dominant, tritone substitutes (climb 10), passing diminished chords. The checker holds you to the landmarks that make it rhythm changes and calls the rest style.

Understand · strains, repeats and the trio

Ragtime was the popular piano music of the USA from about 1895 to 1920, created mainly by African American composers such as Scott Joplin, James Scott and Eubie Blake. Its right hand is syncopated (accents fall between the beats) against a steady left hand that marches: bass, chord, bass, chord.

The form comes from the march. A rag is built from strains: complete 16-bar tunes, each usually repeated. The common plan is Intro, AA BB A, then the trio CC DD. The trio moves to the subdominant key (IV), as in Sousa's marches. Many rags end in the trio key; some, including "Maple Leaf Rag", return home for the last strain (see its score in the Analysis room). Each strain is itself a small double period: 8 bars ending on V, then 8 bars ending with a perfect cadence (see Phrase, period and sentence).

The harmony is common-practice with a popular accent: chains of secondary dominants (VI7–II7–V7–I), passing diminished chords and borrowed iv. Unlike the blues, the dominant 7ths here do resolve. That is the ragtime sound, and it leads straight into stride piano and early jazz.

Understand · the refrain and the journeys between

A rondo alternates one recurring section, the refrain (A), with contrasting episodes (B, C, D). The refrain always returns in the home key; the episodes travel to other keys. The smallest rondo is five-part, ABACA; a seven-part rondo is ABACABA.

It was the favourite form for the last movement of Classical sonatas, symphonies and concertos (Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven): the refrain is usually a cheerful, catchy tune, and every return is a small homecoming. The refrain itself is often a period or a small binary form (see Phrase, period and sentence). A retransition, often a passage sitting on V7, prepares each return.

Compared with verse and chorus. A pop song's chorus also keeps coming back, so the idea is the same, but the Classical rondo makes the key the point: away in the episodes, home for every refrain.
